facts.fact_text: The applicants intended to hold a series of demonstrations between 7 July and 20 August 2004 in front of the Prime Minister's private residence in Budapest.
The applicant stated that the participants in the planned demonstrations intended only to occupy the pedestrian zone across the street from the Prime Minister's house.

Subsequently, the applicant notified the police of another demonstration planned for 1 November 2004, for the same reasons as the earlier demonstrations and at the same spot in front of the Prime Minister's house in Budapest.
The planned number of demonstrators for the 1 November 2004 demonstration was twenty.
Subsequently, the applicants intended to organise other demonstrations limited to twenty persons.

On 18 November 2004 the applicant notified the Budapest Police Department that demonstrations were to take place on 30 November, 1 December, 14 December and in the afternoon of 24 December 2004, again in front of the Prime Minister's house in Budapest.
The applicant stated that his aim was to hold peaceful, silent demonstrations lasting only twenty minutes.
The applicant stated that the only action planned for the demonstrations was to stand in line in front of the Prime Minister's house, with twenty participants.

The Constitution of the Republic of Hungary (Act no. 20 of 1949 as amended), Article 62, provides that the Republic of Hungary acknowledges the right to peaceful assembly and secures its free exercise.
On 5 July 2004 the Budapest Police Department prohibited the planned demonstrations.
In the resumed proceedings following the Budapest Regional Court's decision of 8 July 2004, the Budapest Police Department again prohibited the demonstrations on 10 July 2004.
The head of the Budapest Police Department prohibited the 1 November 2004 demonstration on 28 October 2004, relying on section 8 of Act no. III of 1989 on the Right of Assembly.
On 19 November 2004 the head of the Budapest Police Department prohibited the demonstrations planned for 30 November, 1 December, 14 December and the afternoon of 24 December 2004.
On 8 July 2004 the Budapest Regional Court quashed the Budapest Police Department's decision of 5 July 2004 prohibiting the demonstrations.
On 15 July 2004 the Budapest Regional Court dismissed the applicant's action against the Budapest Police Department's decision of 10 July 2004.
On 5 November 2004 the Budapest Regional Court dismissed the applicant's action against the Budapest Police Department's decision prohibiting the 1 November 2004 demonstration.
On 26 November 2004 the Budapest Regional Court dismissed the applicant's motion seeking judicial review of the Budapest Police Department's decision of 19 November 2004.
The head of the Budapest Police Department prohibited the 1 November 2004 demonstration on 28 October 2004, relying on section 8 of Act no. III of 1989 on the Right of Assembly.
On 19 November 2004 the head of the Budapest Police Department prohibited the demonstrations planned for 30 November, 1 December, 14 December and the afternoon of 24 December 2004.

Section 6 of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly provides that the organisation of an event held in the public domain shall be notified to the competent police headquarters according to the place of the event, and in Budapest to the Budapest Police Headquarters, three days prior to the planned date of the event, and that the obligation to notify the police lies with the organiser of the event.

Section 8(1) of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly (as in force at the relevant time) provides that if the holding of an event subject to prior notification seriously endangers the proper functioning of the representative bodies or courts, or the circulation of traffic cannot be secured by another route, the police may ban the holding of the event at the place or time indicated in the notification, within forty-eight hours of receipt of the notification by the authority.

Section 9(1) of Act no. 3 of 1989 on Freedom of Assembly provides that no appeal shall lie against the decision of the police, but the organiser may seek judicial review of the administrative decision within three days of its notification.

The Budapest Police Department was of the view that the pavement in front of the Prime Minister's house was not wide enough to secure the necessary space for the demonstrators and other pedestrians at the same time.

The Budapest Police Department determined that, in order to prevent possible accidents and confrontations between the demonstrators and passers-by, it would be necessary to close half the street in front of the Prime Minister's house.
The Budapest Police Department pointed out that on the street in front of the Prime Minister's house three bus services operated on a regular basis.
The Budapest Police Department noted that on 1 November 2004, All Saints' Day, the traffic was expected to be heavier since many people would visit cemeteries that day.
The Budapest Police Department held that the 1 November 2004 demonstration would cause a disproportionate hindrance to the traffic, which could not be secured by alternative means.

The Budapest Police Department reiterated that the pavement in front of the Prime Minister's house was not wide enough to secure the necessary space for the demonstrators and other pedestrians at the same time.

The Budapest Police Department determined that, in order to prevent possible accidents and confrontations between the demonstrators and passers-by, half the street in front of the Prime Minister's house would need to be closed.
The Budapest Police Department pointed out that on the street in front of the Prime Minister's house three bus services operated on a regular basis.

The Budapest Police Department noted that in winter, the traffic on the street in front of the Prime Minister's house was expected to be heavier since many people left for the ski resorts around Budapest via that street.
The Budapest Police Department noted that there was a possibility of heavy snowfalls and that it would be difficult to secure alternative routes.

The Budapest Police Department held that the demonstrations planned for 30 November, 1 December, 14 December and 24 December 2004 would cause a disproportionate hindrance to the traffic, in particular to the buses, which could not be secured by alternative means.

According to photographs submitted by the applicant, the Prime Minister's house is situated on a two-lane road in a residential area composed of villas.
Across the street from the Prime Minister's property, between parked cars and the fence of another villa, there is a footpath parallel to which is a strip of grass which is over five metres wide.
